workbooktitle: Recursion with the monks of Mons Komputarius
introduction:
A traveller is looking for a solution for his unsorted cards. The monks show him a way in which a problem keeps getting smaller – and the solution is built on the way back.

Read the story picture by picture; with **Back** and **Next** you can view every step again. In each picture at most one person speaks: **R** is the traveller, **M** the head monk and **K** the child. **...** stands for silent actions and moments of thought.

The cards are inserted on the left on the way back, so the finished row is sorted in **descending** order. Note the traveller's double role: he starts the algorithm and, in the end, also executes the base case.
functionalexplanation: A function’s implementation is called **functional** if it has no mutable state stored outside the function, such as a tally sheet.
warningdialogue: **M:** “That does not surprise me … anyone who rushes into action so quickly will inevitably run past every solution.”
cards-demanddialogue: **R:** “My cards! They need to be sorted!”
journey-questiondialogue: **M:** “My dear stranger … how long did you travel to get here?”
return-questiondialogue: **M:** “And how long will your return journey take?”
patiencedialogue: **M:** “My dear stranger … I can show you our ways. But whether you will understand them … that I cannot promise. They are not difficult … but they require a calmness you seem to lack …”
emptydialogue: **M:** “My dear stranger … you seek solutions, yet you fail to see a solution even when it is right in front of you …”
sorteddialogue: **M:** “My dear stranger. You now know our ways. Go out and use our knowledge whenever you need it. And do not worry: it does not take a temple full of monks to complete the task. Discipline and calm are quite enough!”
understooddialogue: **R:** “I understand completely! I know I can do this on my own. I may not have enough hands … but there is plenty of room on my table. Thank you, great master!”
farewelldialogue: **M:** “I see you have understood. Go now … and approach things a little more calmly in future!”
family-child-questiondialogue: **K:** “Do you know how big it is?”
count-explanationdialogue: **R:** “No, sweetheart … but I know how we can find out!”
kochtitle: 3 · Programming recursion yourself: the Koch curve
kochintroduction:
Now you will program your own recursive algorithm. The **Koch curve** is created by replacing each line segment with four shorter segments: the middle third becomes a triangular peak. The distance from start to finish remains **270 steps**.

Open the editor. You can work in **Python** or with your own **Snap blocks**. Use a function with the parameters **length** and **depth**, and carry it over from one exercise to the next. The preview shows the target drawing and your result. The red arrows in the template indicate directions; they are not part of the drawing.
koch0: Draw a horizontal line **270 steps** to the right. Write a function `koch(length, depth)`. When `depth == 0`, it draws a segment with `forward(length)` and finishes. First call it with length **270** and depth **0**. This is the **base case** of your recursive function.
koch1: Extend the same function: for a greater depth, divide the length by **3** and call `koch` **four times** with the shorter length and a depth reduced by **1**. Between calls, turn **60° left**, **120° right** and **60° left**. Draw the target curve with length **270** and depth **1**. Each of its four segments is **90 steps** long. The turtle faces right again at the end. Use recursive calls rather than four hard-coded `forward` commands.
koch2: Reuse your function from exercise 3b. Change only the depth of the initial call to **2**. Each of the four segments is now replaced by the same pattern again: this produces **16 segments**, each **30 steps** long. Compare your drawing with the target. Check whether you can use the same function for depths **0**, **1** and **2**. As you trace execution, ask yourself: what is simplified, when does a call end, and how do the four partial drawings form the next curve?

zerointro: Before the monks arrive, you get to know the editor. You control a **turtle**: `Turtle.forward(x)` moves it x steps, `Turtle.turnLeft(w)` and `Turtle.turnRight(w)` turn it by w degrees to the left or right. It starts facing right. `Turtle.penUp()` and `Turtle.penDown()` lift and lower the pen. When your drawing matches the target drawing, this is shown. The editor uses **Java**; you can also switch to Python or Snap!.
e1prompt:
The turtle should draw a **building brick**: a rectangle, 60 wide and 20 high. The first half is already given. Complete the rest.

*Target drawing:* a 60 × 20 rectangle; the lower left corner is the starting point.
e2prompt:
1. Write a method `stein(breite)` that draws a brick of the given width and height 20. Afterwards, the turtle must be back at the starting point, facing right.
2. Write a method `hoch()` that moves the turtle up by 20 **without drawing**. It keeps facing right.
3. Use them to draw three stacked bricks of widths 80, 60 and 40 (starting at the bottom, all left-aligned).

*Hint:* lift the pen with `Turtle.penUp()`, lower it with `Turtle.penDown()`.
e3prompt:
Write a method `vieleck(ecken, laenge)` that draws a regular polygon. Use a loop. Draw a square (side length 60) and, to its right, a hexagon (side length 40).

*Hint:* after a full round, the turtle has turned by 360° in total.

*Target drawing:* a 60 × 60 square from the start; a hexagon with side length 40 starting 100 units further to the right.
schemaintro: All recursive solutions of the monks follow the same scheme. Note: the simplification produces **two** things, the separated part and the rest.

a8intro: The traveller says: “I don't have enough hands … but there is enough room on my table.”

countingend:
**How the story ends:** The traveller takes the top brick from the tower, puts it on the table and makes a tally mark. This goes on until nothing is left of the tower. He counts the marks: *“Three bricks, my darling!”*

The child is horrified: *“But now my tower is broken!”* The traveller smiles: *“Don't worry. The table remembered everything.”* He puts the top brick from the pile on the table back on the floor, the next one on top of it, and so on – until the tower stands exactly as before.

Grandma smiles: *“The monks wouldn't have needed a piece of paper for this.”*

c1-row1: He makes a tally mark on the tally list.

c1-row4: He puts the bricks from the table back together into the tower.

c3prompt: Here are three Java methods that count the bricks of a tower. A tower is a string, each character is a brick (e.g. `"RGB"`). `turm.substring(1)` is the tower without its top brick. Assign the matching variant to each description.
c3-row0: The traveller keeps the tally list on a piece of paper next to the table.
c3-row1: The paper with the tally list is passed on with the tower at every step.
c3-row2: The monks: each one puts a brick on the tray when handing it back.

c4-row3: d) `zaehleC("RGB")` is called twice in a row. What does the second call return?

e4prompt:
Now the turtle draws a tower. Write a **recursive** method `zeichneTurm(n)` that draws a tower of `n` bricks of width 40. Do not use a loop.

- If the tower has no bricks, there is nothing to do.
- Otherwise: draw a brick, go up by 20, then draw the rest of the tower (one brick fewer).

*Target drawing:* 5 stacked rectangles of 40 × 20.
e5prompt:
Write a recursive method `zeichnePyramide(n)`. The main program uses it to draw two pyramids next to each other. The second one only ends up in the right place if the turtle is back at its starting point after the first pyramid.

- For `n == 0` there is nothing to do.
- Otherwise: draw a brick of width `n * 20`. Then go up by 20 and right by 10 and draw a pyramid with `n - 1` layers.
- **Afterwards**, move the turtle back 10 to the left and 20 down so that it stands where the call began.

*Target drawing:* on the left a pyramid of 4 layers (widths 80, 60, 40, 20, each indented by 10), next to it from x = 100 on the same baseline a pyramid of 3 layers.
e6aprompt:
The program should draw the same two pyramids as in E5, but it does not. Find the error and fix it.

*Expected:* the drawing never stops (bricks with negative width) until the editor reports the execution limit. In plain Java this ends with a `StackOverflowError`.
e6bprompt:
The program should draw the same two pyramids as in E5, but it does not. Find the error and fix it.

*Expected:* the second pyramid floats at the upper right instead of standing on the baseline.
d1a-question: Where is the turtle right after the call `zeichnePyramide(3)` (sample solution of E5)?
d1a-opt0: On the top layer of the pyramid
d1a-opt1: At the same point and facing the same direction as before the call
d1a-opt2: That depends on how large `n` is
d1a-opt3: To the right of the bottom layer
d1b-question: `zeichnePyramide(4)` calls `zeichnePyramide(3)`. What must the call with 4 be able to rely on?
d1b-opt0: That the turtle is at the very top after the call.
d1b-opt1: That a pyramid with 3 layers is drawn.
d1b-opt2: That the call with 3 also draws the bottom layer.
d1b-opt3: That the turtle is afterwards back where the call with 3 began.
d1b-opt4: That the call with 3 knows how wide the layer below it is.
d1note: As with the monks, every call has a **contract**: you only think about your own level and rely on the contract of the call.
d2-row0: a) How often is `f` called in total for `f(3)` (counting the first call)?
d2-row1: b) How many lines are drawn for `f(3)`?
d2-row2: c) Instead of twice, the method now calls itself **three times**. How many lines are drawn for `f(2)`?
e7prompt:
Write a recursive method `cantor(laenge, n)` that draws the following pattern: a line; below it only the left and the right third of this line; below that again the left and right third of each of those, and so on.

- Draw a line of length `laenge` (helper method `linie`).
- If `n == 0`, you are done.
- Otherwise: go down by 20 and call `cantor` for the **left third** with a third of the length and `n - 1`.
- Then go right by two thirds of the length and do the same for the **right third**.
- Finally, bring the turtle back to where the call began.

*Target drawing:* 4 levels, 20 apart: one line of length 270; two lines of 90; four lines of 30; eight lines of 10.
e7b-caption: How many lines are drawn in total for `cantor(270, 3)`?
e8prompt:
Write a recursive method `baum(laenge, n)` that draws a tree. A tree consists of a trunk on which two smaller trees grow: one tilted to the left, one to the right.

- For `n == 0` there is nothing to do.
- Otherwise: draw the trunk (`laenge` forward).
- Turn 30° to the left and draw a tree with 60 % of the length and `n - 1`.
- Turn 60° to the right and draw another such tree.
- Turn the turtle back to the original direction and bring it back to the foot of the trunk.

*Target drawing:* a symmetric binary tree with 5 levels, trunk length 80, branching angle ±30°, length factor 0.6.
